21.0.0.en: Judgments: laws that God set down in His high wisdom.

21.0.1.en: God gave Moses not only the Ten Commandments but a law, or Law, covering people's conduct in various respects, and the first thing it speaks of in the Law is servants, because this system prevailed in the world at that time. The Law provides that the Hebrew servant be treated with love, for he is a servant for a temporary period of six years at most, and in the seventh year he is set free.

21.0.2.en: The number (7) signifies the work of the Holy Spirit, who convicts us of every sin and forgives it for us and so frees us from it. This law declares that the servant is not owned like a piece of furniture or an animal but is so for a temporary period, in order to change the idea of enslavement within man and free him from it, and on the other hand it eases the lot of the servants who have been sold to their masters because of poverty.

21.0.3.en: It also confirms the value of faith, for this law applies to the Hebrew only, to declare that faith frees us from bondage.

21.1.0.en: The Law also provides for respect for the servant's property: if he was married before his servitude, then when he is set free he takes his wife with him; but if his master had given him one of the maidservants to marry and he had children by her, he goes out alone and leaves his wife and children, because they are not his own but his master's. So this law declares the importance of respecting the property of others and of not exploiting opportunities to control others.

21.2.0.en: "The judges": what is meant is the judges who sit near the gate of the city and judge by the law of God.

21.2.1.en: If the servant chooses of his own will to remain with his wife and children because of his emotional attachment to them and his comfort in serving his master, he remains a servant all his life with this master. Here this matter must be declared before the whole city, that is, before the judges or elders of the city who sit in its square at its entrance, and he brings him to the gate of the city before all those entering and going out, or to the door post of the city gate (the side of the door), and bores his ear through, so that it will be a visible sign before the people, in order to protect the servant who did not wish to continue in his master's servitude, so that his master may not come and say that this servant of mine agreed to be with me all his life when this has not actually happened, since they will not find a hole in his ear. He chose the ear as a conspicuous organ in man, concerned with hearing, that is, to declare his readiness to obey his master all his life.

21.2.2.en: And the servant's choosing to remain with his master all his life is a reference to the spiritual man's accepting, in the New Testament, to be a servant of Christ, who bought him with His blood, in order to enjoy God's care and fellowship with his fellow believers (his wife and children), or for the sanctification of his body and his senses, which the wife and children signify.

21.3.0.en: If a Hebrew man becomes poor and sells his daughter as a maidservant and her master marries her, she does not go out after the period of servitude has ended, but remains a free wife with her master, who has become her husband, and lives with him as a free woman. But if she was merely a maidservant and not a wife, she goes out in the seventh year or the year of jubilee and is freed. Thus, when she leaves her father's house for her master, she is honored as a servant in the house and not a slave, because she stays with her master for a period until her father or her kin are able to redeem her and pay her price, or she is let go free in the seventh year and returns with honor to her father's house.

21.4.0.en: If a master marries his maidservant and then wants to divorce her, he cannot sell her to anyone but is bound to care for her and provide for her, because he has taken pleasure in marrying her; this marriage must be respected, for it is not merely a pleasure or a personal benefit.

21.4.1.en: Here appears respect for marriage even before Christianity declared it a holy sacrament, and also the husband's responsibility for his wife, even if she was a maidservant, so that he cares for her and her feelings, for she is not an instrument of pleasure as the Gentiles treat her. That is, if he wants to separate from her and divorce her, he frees her to marry a Hebrew man and not a Gentile, and he also does not sell her to a Gentile man, because he took pleasure in living with her, so he has no right to sell her as a maidservant, since he did not keep her as a mere maidservant.

21.5.0.en: Among the rights of the maidservant whom the master marries to his son is that he give her her dowry of jewels or possessions and hold a wedding celebration for her like the other girls who are not maidservants.

21.5.1.en: Here is a confirmation of respect for the servant's property and also esteem for her feelings, for the dowry or the betrothal gift is a proof of the husband's love for his wife. But if the maidservant lived with her master's son and was set free in the seventh year, she lives after that as an honored wife and not a maidservant, and if he divorces her she is treated as a free woman and takes all her possessions.

21.6.0.en: If the master wants to marry another woman, he is bound to take care of his first wife in providing for her and in his bodily union with her, but if he refuses, he frees her. Here we see that although custom and the Law permitted a plurality of wives, they respected the first marriage even if it was to a maidservant, and if the husband neglected his responsibility for his wife, he frees her as a punishment to him for his neglect, that is, he does not sell her to anyone. We notice from (Neh 5:5-8) that after the captivity the bondage of the Hebrews to one another was abolished.

21.6.1.en: Would that you would feel your responsibility toward those around you and give them their rights before you demand duties of them, and if you wrong them, you should apologize and compensate them for any harm that resulted from your wronging them.

21.7.0.en: The life of man is the most precious thing, therefore whoever despises it is punished with a like punishment, so whoever kills deliberately must be put to death. The Law teaches the importance of respecting the lives of others and of not wronging them, whether bodily, psychologically or spiritually, as Christianity explained in more detail (Mt 5:21-26).

21.8.0.en: Whoever kills another by accident, "God deliver him into his hand," is not put to death, because he did not intend to kill him, and God appointed cities to which this killer may flee (the cities of refuge), which God determined to Moses and Joshua carried out (Num 35:6-15; Josh 20); they signify Christ, to whom we take refuge, and He protects us and removes from us the punishment of our sins. This killer is sufficiently punished by being deprived of his family, his possessions and his work, and this is a temporary punishment until the great priest dies or the year of jubilee, that is, the fiftieth, comes, and he is freed and no one can take revenge on him. The death of the great priest signifies the death of Christ, who frees us from the bondage of sin.

21.8.1.en: This sin is a sin of laxity, so it has a punishment, but not like the punishment of murder.

21.9.0.en: "The altar of God" means the bronze altar on which the burnt offerings are offered in the tabernacle of the congregation, the details of whose construction God will give to Moses after this speech.

21.9.1.en: And the altar represents the presence of God among His people and His keeping and rescuing them from every danger, because upon it is the sacrifice that signifies the Redeemer and Savior. If a man kills another deliberately he must be put to death, because he despised his brother's life, as mentioned in (v. 12), and even if he hastens to the altar and clings to it, he is taken and put to death, because the one who killed his brother unintentionally would take refuge at the altar until the judges examined him, and if that was established he would go to the cities of refuge, but if it was deliberate he must be put to death, as happened in the days of Solomon when Joab clung to the horns of the altar (1 Kgs 2:28-32).

21.10.0.en: It moves to another law besides killing, which is striking, and begins with a son's striking his father or his mother; for the sake of their great honor, as the fifth commandment states, this son must be put to death. From here is understood the confirmation of honoring parents and respecting their feelings and not wronging them in any way, even if they err.

21.11.0.en: He speaks here of another sin, which is theft, and chooses from it the hardest, which is stealing a man and selling him as a slave; this is a contempt for a man's life that approaches the sin of murder, so the Law sentences this thief to death.

21.11.1.en: Do not steal the rights of others to express their opinion or their freedom of movement, life and choice, even if your aim is good, because God Himself does not force His children to live with Him but calls them to Him in every way, in addition to the fact that man cannot bear the loss of his freedom all his life.

21.12.0.en: He points here to another sin, which is cursing when it is directed at the nearest of kin, the parents; it is an insult and a robbing of their honor, so it also approaches the sin of murder, therefore the Law sentences the curser to death.

21.12.1.en: Do not persist in your anger so that words insulting to others come out of your mouth, for by this you kill them morally and not physically, and this too is a hard matter and leads to many psychological troubles. So do not be lax in this, relying on their being members of your household or under your authority, for this is a hard sin before God and its punishment is great. And remember that your basic work is to encourage others to draw near to God and to do constructive work.

21.13.0.en: He returns again to the sin of striking, using any means such as a stick or stones; if that leads to the other's death, the striker is put to death, as mentioned in (v. 12), but if he is sick for a time in his house, the striker is not put to death but compensates the one struck by paying his wages for the days of his being kept from work and also the cost of his treatment.

21.13.1.en: If you have wronged a person you must compensate him for the harm of your wronging him. If you insulted him with words of cursing, you must apologize to him, and if the insult was in front of people, the apology should also be in front of people, and if any material harm befell him, he must be compensated more than what befell him; this is a proof of your repentance and your love.

21.14.0.en: The law of striking included masters with their servants, so out of sanctification of man's life, even if he is a servant, if his striking by his master led to his death, vengeance is taken on his master. What is meant by vengeance is his punishment, and most likely his being put to death or his paying a large fine, as the judges or elders decide. The Gentiles considered the servant part of the master's property and held that it was his right to kill him if he wished.

21.15.0.en: If a master strikes his servant and he lives a day or two, vengeance is not taken on him, first because he did not intend to kill him and second because his material loss in losing his servant is enough for him.

21.15.1.en: But in the first case, which is the death of the servant, vengeance is taken on the master because he went beyond discipline in his striking and was violent to the point of killing.

21.16.0.en: If a quarrel occurs between men and they strike a woman with child so that her unborn child comes out, its growth not having been completed inside her womb, this is considered a sin of killing without intent but of a human being not yet complete, therefore the men are not put to death and do not flee to the cities of refuge, but they pay a fine as the judges decide, after the husband demands what he wants.

21.16.1.en: This is a sin of negligence and violent anger that led to a fight, therefore the wrongdoer is punished with a fine according to the circumstances of each case and the extent of the harm that occurred and the violence of the quarrel.

21.17.0.en: If the men's colliding with the woman with child led to her falling and dying, those who struck her are put to death; this is a sin of killing without intent but connected with the sin of violent anger that led to a quarrel which ended a human life, so it is different from the sin of killing without intent mentioned in (v. 13) because it is connected with violent anger.

21.18.0.en: If harm is done to the woman with child by the quarrelers and one of her members is injured or lost, such as the eye, the tooth, the hand or the foot, then whoever struck her is punished by having his eye put out or one of his teeth, or his hand or foot cut off, and he may compensate by a suitable fine as the judges decide.

21.18.1.en: And this law declares justice and the bearing of responsibility, so that man may take care not to harm another, or he will be punished with the same harm.

21.18.2.en: St. Augustine divided dealings between people into five degrees, which are:

21.18.3.en: 1- Attacking the other and harming him, and this is what happens among barbarous peoples.

21.18.4.en: 2- Wronging the wrongdoer with a greater harm because he is the one who began.

21.18.5.en: 3- Wronging the wrongdoer with the same amount of harm that he caused, as in Judaism.

21.18.6.en: 4- Wronging the wrongdoer and harming him with a lesser harm, and this is what happens among higher peoples, if the one who was wronged is distressed and expresses his distress with some wrong.

21.18.7.en: 5- Forgiving the wrongdoer and pitying him as a sick man, and even offering him love, and this is the highest conduct, as in Christianity.

21.18.8.en: And this law points to the matter of redemption, since every harm needs a like compensation, and man's unlimited sin needs unlimited atonement and unlimited compensation, and this was accomplished in Christ's death for us on the Cross. By this law the victim was prevented from taking vengeance beyond the harm that befell him: if his eye was injured, for example, he does not take vengeance by more than hurting the other's eye. But what used to happen in any attack was that the elders would estimate the amount of the injury and fine the attacker the suitable price, which he pays to the victim (Num 35:21-25).

21.19.0.en: He continues the kinds of harm and the compensation for them with their equivalents, which are:

21.19.1.en: 1- Whoever uses a hot metal tool to burn the skin of another (a brand) is dealt with as he has done.

21.19.2.en: 2- Whoever wounds another so that blood flows from him is punished with the same punishment.

21.19.3.en: 3- Whoever strikes another so that bruises (contusions) occur is struck until like bruises occur on him.

21.20.0.en: If a master strikes his servant and causes him to lose his eye or one of his teeth, then in compensation for this harm he lets him go free.

21.21.0.en: If a person approaches an ox without caution and it gores him and he dies, the ox is put to death, to show the importance of human life, but the owner of the ox is not punished because he intended no evil, and it was the one killed who approached the ox without care. And the flesh of the ox is not eaten, because it was not slaughtered in the natural way but was killed by stoning, so its blood is in it, and it signifies aggression and evil.

21.21.1.en: Care about the lives and feelings of others more than about your property and your comfort. Do not be selfish and cause harm unintentionally through your preoccupation with your work or your trade or your personal mood, such as making noise or exploiting your ability in trade so that you press on others until they lose their trade entirely; rather, be merciful and consider the feelings of others.

21.22.0.en: If the ox was one that often gored and had harmed others before, and its owner was warned by many and did not restrain it or slaughter it but left it to harm others until it killed a person, the Law decrees that the ox be put to death and its owner also, because he despises the lives of people and is immersed in his selfishness, caring about his property more than about the lives of others.

21.23.0.en: If the relatives of the one killed agree to accept a ransom for the dead man, then as the elders estimate, the owner must pay this fine as compensation for the killing of the person whom the ox gored.

21.24.0.en: If the one killed by the ox's goring is young in age, his life is not made light of because of his youth, but the owner of the ox is put to death if his ox was one that often gored and he had been warned, with the killing of the ox; but if the ox was not a goring one, only the ox is put to death.

21.25.0.en: A shekel of silver: equal to about 360 g - 450 g of silver.

21.25.1.en: If the ox gores a manservant or a maidservant and kills him, the master is compensated with the price of the servant, which is thirty shekels of silver, and the ox is stoned to death, to show the importance of human life.

21.26.0.en: If a person is negligent, having opened one of the old wells for drinking and after drinking from it did not cover it with a stone, or if he dug a new well and after drinking from it did not cover it with a stone, and one of the animals such as an ox or an ass fell into it, this negligent person is punished by paying a fine, which is the price of this ox or ass, and this negligent person takes the dead animal to benefit from its hide or its fleece or anything in it.

21.26.1.en: Beware of negligence that harms others, whether in your work or your speech, and if it happens you must compensate, and an apology is not enough; and as you want others not to neglect you, do not neglect them either.

21.27.0.en: If an ox gores another animal such as another ox and it dies, the ox that gored is sold and they divide its price, that is, the owner of the ox that gored and the owner of the ox that was killed, and likewise the dead ox is sold and they divide its price.

21.28.0.en: If an ox gores another ox and it is known that the ox was a goring one and its owner was warned before witnesses and did nothing, he is punished by compensating the owner of the dead ox by giving him an ox like it, and then this negligent man takes the dead ox to benefit from its remains.

21.28.1.en: Laws of theft, adultery, cursing and other laws
